doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The aging audience and media neglect
summary: Ingham notes the small, older audience for his kind of jazz and that TV shows like Letterman ignore it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well there is. It’s small and I guess it seems to get smaller. If you look at the audience today, most of these people, God bless them, are not in the first bloom of youth. And if only we could reach younger people. I mean the players are pretty young some of them. I mean we’re not teenagers, but we still think we’ve got something to offer. And we sort of work within a tradition and try to do your own thing with it, which I don’t see anything wrong in that. And instead of trying to be as modern — modern is such a silly word, because what’s modern today gets very dated. And I think if you look back to the things that were considered very innovative at the time, a lot of that Stan Kenton stuff, is dated terribly, and that kind of beboppy, scat singing with the guy [scats]. It sounds so corny. It’s like those silly old suits, those zoot suits of theirs that nobody would wear. But the really good stuff stays. And I don’t think you should aim to be timeless, but just if you’re doing it true to yourself and not going for these sort of effects, and trying to be hip all the time, something will come through. But I do wish, I mean that’s where the media could help in a way, but would you ever see a band like ours on David Letterman? No way. Or would you ever see us on even an early morning show? No. It’s sadly no. Because these people don’t know. These guys that produce these programs don’t know. They grew up with The Rolling Stones or probably even like Led Zeppelin and some that came afterwards.
The Rolling Stones are old now.
